the genetic contribution to risk of problem-drinking behavior is significant, but that the size of that contribution is variable and depends on the particular model of analysis used.

there is a moderate degree of genetic influence on alcohol consumption level and problem drinking in both males and females, and that genetic influences on level of consumption and problem drinking are moderately correlated in both sexes.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

there is a substantial genetic contribution to the risk of problem drinking, but that the genetic contribution to risk of problem alcohol use is not entirely explained by the genetic contribution to alcohol consumption level.

there is significant genetic influence on risk for problem drinking and that this genetic influence is correlated with genetic influences on alcohol consumption level, although the strength of the correlation is not as great as that between genetic influences on consumption level and consumption level itself.

genetic factors play a major role in determining both level of alcohol consumption and problem drinking in both sexes, but that the magnitude of the heritability estimates for the latter are less consistent and less clearly defined.
The main takeaway from our work is that
there is a significant genetic contribution to the risk of problem drinking.
genetic factors are important in the etiology of both alcohol consumption and problem drinking, and that there is a significant genetic correlation between these traits.
the genetic influences on alcohol consumption level are not the same as the genetic influences on the risk of problem drinking.
